name: Panankatteeswarar Temple, Panaiyapuram
deity: Shiva as Panankatteeswarar (Panankatteesar), with the goddess Sathyambikai (Puravammai)
period: Ancient Shaiva shrine of the Nadu Nadu country, sung in the Tevaram (7th century); Pallava origins rebuilt in stone under the Cholas
dynasty: Pallava origins, rebuilt in stone by the Cholas
summary: Panankatteeswarar is the Shiva temple of Panaiyapuram, the Puravar Panankattur of the Tevaram, a Paadal Petra Sthalam of the Nadu Nadu country praised by Tirugnana Sambandar and remembered for the Sun who regained his radiance in worship here.

sections.history: Panaiyapuram, the palm-town of the Nadu Nadu country west of Villupuram, is an old Shiva shrine known to the Tevaram as Puravar Panankattur, the palm-forest of Puravar. The hymns of Tirugnana Sambandar, gathered in the Second Thirumurai, praise the Lord here, which makes the temple a Paadal Petra Sthalam, counted among the shrines of the Nadu Nadu group. Tradition holds that the Lord first appeared amid a grove of palms, and the palm remains the temple's sacred tree. The shrine is understood to have risen in the Pallava age, before the time of the hymns, and to have been rebuilt in stone in the Chola period, after which it has been kept in worship across the centuries.
sections.architecture: The temple is a modest east-facing shrine of the Nadu Nadu countryside, its sanctum holding the linga of Panankatteeswarar within walls of granite, with the goddess Sathyambikai, also called Puravammai, honoured in her own shrine. The temple is best known for a feat of orientation rather than of height: for the first several days of the Tamil month of Chithirai, when the new year turns, the rising sun sends its light through the eastern doorway to fall first upon the Lord in the sanctum and then upon the goddess, a solar alignment built into the very placing of the shrine. Beyond this the temple keeps the plain dignity of a village foundation rather than the ornament of the great temples of the plains.
sections.legends: The temple's great story is the Sun's. Surya, having gone to the sacrifice of Daksha that Shiva's rite did not favour, is said to have lost his brightness as a consequence and to have come to this place to worship the Lord and win back his radiance. From his penance the shrine keeps its bond with the Sun, and the yearly alignment of light upon the sanctum at the turn of the year is read as the Lord's grace to Surya made visible. The name Panankattur, the palm forest, is tied to the grove in which the Lord is said to have first revealed himself, and the palm is honoured as the sacred tree to this day.
sections.festivals: The temple's signature observance is the alignment of the sun upon the sanctum in the first days of Chithirai, in April, when the rising light falls upon the Lord and then the goddess and is kept with special worship. Maha Shivaratri and the monthly Pradosham are observed as at every Shiva temple. As the calendar is the Tamil one and the fuller festival round of this village shrine is not widely recorded, confirm the days and the details locally before travelling.
sections.experience: Panaiyapuram is a quiet country temple, visited more by the devout of the surrounding villages than by crowds, and it rewards an unhurried call. Come to the sanctum of Panankatteeswarar and then to the goddess Sathyambikai in her shrine, and if the visit falls in the first days of Chithirai, the alignment of the sunrise upon the Lord is the sight to seek. The palm, the temple's sacred tree, recalls the grove of the name and the Sun's penance, and the plainness of the shrine is in keeping with its age and its setting among the fields.

visit.timings: Typically open for a few hours in the morning and again in the evening, with a long midday closure; as a village temple the hours can vary, so confirm locally before visiting, especially around the Chithirai sun-alignment days.
visit.dressCode: Modest traditional attire is expected: dhotis or trousers for men, sarees, salwar kameez, or long skirts for women, with shoulders and knees covered. Footwear is left at the entrance stands.
visit.photography: Photography is generally permitted in the outer courtyards but prohibited inside the inner sanctum, in keeping with Tamil Nadu temple rules. Ask temple staff before photographing rituals or priests.
visit.gettingThere: Panaiyapuram lies in Villupuram district, about 13 km from Villupuram and near Vikravandi and Mundiyampakkam, reached by local roads off the Villupuram highways. Villupuram, the nearest major railway junction and bus hub, is the practical base; local buses and road transport serve the village.
